title: Rethinking Channel Estimation for Fluid Antenna Systems: A Physics-Informed Operator Learning

paper.title: Rethinking Channel Estimation for Fluid Antenna Systems: A Physics-Informed Operator Learning
paper.abstract:
Abstract Fluid antenna systems (FAS) leverage continuous reconfigurable apertures to transcend the spatial limits of fixed-position arrays, yet acquiring full-aperture channel state information (CSI) from sparse observations remains a formidable bottleneck. In this paper, we establish a continuous-field formulation for FAS by recasting channel estimation as a stochastic inverse field-reconstruction problem constrained by the projected Helmholtz model. Through electromagnetic information theory (EIT)-based spectral leakage analysis, we demonstrate that finite-aperture reconstruction induces an intrinsic convolutional relationship in the spectral domain, rendering the estimation task a fundamental frequency-domain inverse deconvolution problem.
To solve this, we propose a U-shaped Fourier neural operator (UFNO) specifically tailored for noisy, underdetermined wireless environments. Furthermore, we leverage the Landau–Pollak theorem to derive an aperture-dependent EDoF bound that guides the spatial mode budget, and employ a physics-aware Sobolev loss to promote consistency in both channel values and spatial variations. Unlike conventional learning-based approaches, a single frozen UFNO can be directly evaluated at unseen spatial–frequency resolutions without resolution-specific retraining or explicit output interpolation. Extensive simulations show that our framework significantly outperforms state-of-the-art benchmarks in accuracy while achieving orders-of-magnitude lower inference latency than iterative solvers at high spatial–frequency resolutions .

sections.heading: I Introduction
sections.text: Multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) technology is fundamental to contemporary wireless networks, leveraging spatial degrees of freedom (DoFs) to enhance spectral efficiency and link reliability [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 ] . However, conventional MIMO architectures are inherently limited by the Nyquist-based half-wavelength spacing rule, which restricts spatial diversity gains within a fixed physical aperture regardless of antenna density. To surpass these constraints, continuous-aperture MIMO (CAP-MIMO) has emerged as a transformative paradigm [ 5 , 3 ] . By integrating metasurfaces or dense sub-wavelength arrays, CAP-MIMO enables ultra-fine electromagnetic (EM) control, effectively realizing a holographic radiating aperture [ 5 ] . Nevertheless, translating the theoretical potential of CAP-MIMO into practice is hindered by several interrelated challenges. The extreme proximity of sub-wavelength elements induces severe mutual coupling and complex near-field interactions that complicate signal processing. Furthermore, acquiring full-space EM channel state information (CSI) necessitates high-dimensional channel matrices, where the resulting “curse of dimensionality” imposes prohibitive pilot and computational overheads. These difficulties are compounded by the excessive hardware costs and power consumption associated with scaling active elements, presenting substantial barriers to the large-scale commercialization of dense-array-centric architectures. Against this backdrop, fluid antenna systems (FAS) introduce a transformative paradigm that sidesteps the limitations of static hardware densification [ 6 , 7 , 8 , 9 ] . By enabling a limited number of movable antennas to dynamically traverse a continuous spatial manifold within a predefined aperture, FAS not only minimizes hardware overhead but also circumvents the analytical complexities and hardware redundancy inherent in metasurface-based CAP-MIMO. The seminal work in [ 10 ] first introduced the FAS concept, and demonstrated that even a small linear aperture (e.g., 0.5 λ \lambda ) with sub-wavelength port spacing can yield significant spatial diversity gains, even surpassing multi-antenna MRC systems. Furthermore, the authors in [ 11 ] revealed that FAS can achieve substantial ergodic capacity in both point-to-point and multi-user multiple-access scenarios. However, FAS performance hinges on high-resolution CSI across the full spatial domain, demanding dense sub-wavelength measurements. Hardware constraints permit only a sparse subset, rendering channel estimation a severely underdetermined inverse problem. Considering its sparse nature, a conventional approach is adopting compressed sensing (CS) technology [ 12 , 13 , 14 ] . By sending pilots from the random antenna ports, the channel estimation problem can be formulated as a sparse signal recovery problem, which can be solved by algorithms such as orthogonal matching pursuit (OMP) or sparse Bayesian learning (SBL). For instance, the authors in [ 12 ] proposed a successive transmitter-receiver compressed sensing (STRCS) method by exploiting the angular-domain sparsity of multi-path components to reconstruct the continuous field-response information from finite measurements. The authors in [ 13 ] developed an SBL-based channel estimator by reformulating the estimation task into a basis selection problem, thereby achieving superior reconstruction accuracy with limited radio-frequency chains. However, these methods are fundamentally limited by the discretization of the channel into a finite grid, leading to grid mismatch artifacts and high computational complexity in high-dimensional scenarios. Besides, these methods highly rely on the sparsity assumption based on the shallow scattering environment, leading to limited implementation cases. Conversely, learning-based approaches leverage data-driven architectures to characterize the nonlinear mapping from sparse pilot observations to full-space channel realizations, thereby shifting the burden of computationally intensive iterations to low-latency feed-forward inference. Beyond conventional neural network-driven channel extrapolation, which seeks to learn direct mappings from sparse inputs to high-dimensional CSI, the reconstruction of the channel field via generative modeling has emerged as a pivotal research frontier. Frameworks such as diffusion models [ 15 ] , conditional generative adversarial networks (cGANs) [ 16 ] , and variational autoencoders (VAEs) [ 17 ] reformulate channel estimation as an inverse problem regularized by learned implicit priors. These methods have demonstrated a superior capacity for capturing intricate electromagnetic (EM) characteristics and spatial correlations at sub-wavelength scales. Despite their reconstructive fidelity, diffusion-based methods necessitate multi-step iterative sampling, which incurs substantial computational latency. This delay poses a significant challenge in satisfying the stringent constraints of the channel coherence interval, particularly in high-mobility scenarios. Furthermore, while techniques based on 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS), such as RF-PGS [ 18 ] , RF-3DGS [ 19 ] , facilitate rapid rendering and geometric alignment, they are fundamentally limited to site-specific optimization. These approaches lack the generalization capability required for inference in unseen environments and often neglect the underlying physical operator constraints governing electromagnetic wave propagation. Grounded in electromagnetic information theory (EIT) [ 5 , 20 , 21 , 22 ] , wireless channels are fundamentally modeled as continuous physical fields governed by Maxwell’s equations and the associated Helmholtz equation, rather than as collections of isolated random variables. Although these fields exhibit an inherent low-rank structure in the wavenumber domain, existing solution methodologies encounter significant technical barriers. Specifically, numerical solvers, e.g., ray tracing, the finite element method, and the finite-difference method, are often computationally prohibitive. Moreover, they are constrained by a prohibitive trade-off between computational accuracy and efficiency, making them ill-suited for the millisecond-level real-time reconstruction required by 6G networks. Alternatively, statistical kernel-based approaches [ 20 ] , including Gaussian process regression and kernel learning, have introduced physically inspired kernels, such as the electromagnetic correlation function. However, these methods essentially rely on fixed-kernel structures, which lead to high computational complexity for matrix inversion and struggle to adapt to complex, dynamic EM environments. Furthermore, most existing techniques lack resolution invariance, limiting direct channel reconstruction at spatial–frequency discretizations unseen during training. Inspired by the paradigm shift toward neural operator learning for partial differential equations (PDEs) [ 23 ] , we propose a physics-informed learning framework tailored for FAS channel estimation. Unlike deterministic and noise-free PDE benchmarks where Fourier Neural Operators (FNOs) excel, FAS estimation presents an ill-posed inverse problem with an unknown stochastic excitation and severely undersampled observations. Standard FNOs can not be directly implemented for this problem due to their rigid spectral truncation, which lacks adaptability to varying noise levels, and a pervasive low-pass bias that suppresses critical sub-wavelength spatial features. To address these challenges, we reformulate FAS channel estimation as a continuous operator learning task and introduce a U-shaped FNO (UFNO) whose non-local architecture is motivated by the projected Helmholtz model. The primary contributions of this work are summarized as follows. ∙ \bullet We recast FAS channel estimation as a stochastic inverse field-reconstruction problem constrained by the projected Helmholtz model. By shifting from discrete vector recovery to continuous field reconstruction, we utilize EIT to reveal that finite-aperture sensing induces an intrinsic spectral convolution. This analysis formalizes the channel estimation task as an inverse deconvolution problem within the spatio-frequency domain. ∙ \bullet Beyond empirical modeling, we derive a closed-form upper bound on the effective degrees of freedom (EDoF) of the FAS channel via the Landau–Pollak theorem. This result characterizes the aperture-dependent spatial dimensionality and provides a physics-based reference for selecting the UFNO spatial mode budget. We further distinguish this ideal dimension count from SNR-dependent stable recovery through a finite-aperture singular-value analysis and multi-aperture simulations. ∙ \bullet We develop a UFNO based channel estimation framework to overcome the limitations of conventional operators through two key mechanisms. First, a learnable soft-thresholding operator is introduced to dynamically suppress noise while preserving physical signal modes across varying signal-to-noise ratios (SNRs). Second, a dual-branch spectral-spatial structure is employed to mitigate low-pass bias, enabling the simultaneous capture of macroscopic low-frequency structures and high-frequency sub-wavelength details. ∙ \bullet We propose a physics-aware Sobolev loss that penalizes discrepancies in both channel values and spatial–frequency variations. This regularization enhances the recovery of high-gradient scattering structures. Numerical results demonstrate that our framework achieves grid-agnostic reconstruction with orders-of-magnitude lower latency than model-based baselines. The rest of the paper is organized as follows. Section II introduces the system model and FAS channel modeling. Section III details the proposed UFNO framework, including its architecture and loss function design. Section IV presents simulation results comparing UFNO with benchmark methods. Finally, Section V concludes the paper.

sections.heading: II System Model and Modeling of FAS Channels
sections.text: This section establishes a physics-informed model in which the continuous aperture field is characterized by a projected stochastic Helmholtz relation. By analyzing the resulting spatio-frequency structure, we establish the motivation for operator learning.

sections.heading: II-C From Physical Principles to Operator Learning
sections.text: To characterize the intrinsic structure of the reconstruction problem posed in ( 5 ), we analyze it from two complementary perspectives: the spectral domain and the spatial domain. Regarding the spectral domain, under the source-free condition (i.e., the homogeneous counterpart of ( 4 )), the field exhibits a strictly band-limited structure in classical wave theory [ 21 ] , with spectral energy mathematically confined to a bounded support. Theoretically, this property guarantees perfect field reconstruction via Nyquist-compliant sampling. However, while the global EM field is band-limited, an FAS receiver only observes this field over a finite, continuous aperture 𝒮 = [ 0 , L ] \mathcal{S}=[0,L] . Mathematically, this finite-aperture observation process is formulated as: H obs ​ ( s , f ) = H ∞ ​ ( s , f ) ⋅ rect ​ ( s − L / 2 L ) , H_{\text{obs}}(s,f)=H_{\infty}(s,f)\cdot\text{rect}\left(\frac{s-L/2}{L}\right), (7) where H ∞ ​ ( s , f ) H_{\infty}(s,f) denotes the ideal field of infinite extent, and rect ​ ( ⋅ ) \text{rect}(\cdot) is the rectangular window function. Specifically, the convolution inherently produces non-zero spectral components that spill beyond the theoretical cutoff wavenumber κ ⁡ ( f ) \kappa(f) , causing the observed field to deviate from the ideal band-limited assumption. Equivalently, for each frequency offset f f , this convolution relationship reveals a fundamental insight: reconstructing the latent clean spectrum H ^ ∞ ​ ( k s , f ) \hat{H}_{\infty}(k_{s},f) from finite-aperture observations is intrinsically an inverse deconvolution problem in the wavenumber domain . This deficiency is rigorously governed by the Helmholtz equation ( 4 ), which constrains the spatial phase progression of an impinging plane wave to k s = 1 λ ​ cos ⁡ θ k_{s}=\frac{1}{\lambda}\cos\theta . Crucially, because the spatial aperture 𝒮 \mathcal{S} is strictly bounded, the Green’s function is square-integrable over 𝒟 \mathcal{D} . Accordingly, the integral operator constitutes a compact operator on the Hilbert space. Its decaying singular values explain why inversion from noisy finite-aperture observations is ill-conditioned even when the nominal dimension requirement is met. The duality between the spatial differential operator ℒ κ \mathcal{L}_{\kappa} and its inverse ℒ κ − 1 \mathcal{L}_{\kappa}^{-1} therefore motivates a critical shift in perspective: the FAS reconstruction task can be naturally reframed as an operator learning problem over continuous channel fields rather than a resolution-specific vector recovery problem. The resulting neural operator maps sparse measurements to the channel distribution represented in the training data while retaining a non-local integral-operator structure motivated by the Helmholtz model. Remark 1 . The projected Helmholtz relation motivates the operator formulation above rather than serving as a pointwise residual constraint during training. Because ξ ⁡ ( s , f ) \xi(s,f) is an unknown stochastic excitation, imposing the homogeneous residual ‖ ℒ κ ​ H ^ ‖ 2 2 \|\mathcal{L}_{\kappa}\widehat{H}\|_{2}^{2} would incorrectly force this excitation to zero; moreover, the sparse pilot samples are measurement constraints within 𝒟 \mathcal{D} rather than prescribed Dirichlet or Neumann boundary values on ∂ 𝒟 \partial\mathcal{D} . Thus, the proposed UFNO incorporates physics through the continuous-field model and the associated operator structure, without explicit PDE-residual enforcement. Remark 2 . The quantity N DoF = ⌈ 2 ​ W ⌉ + 1 N_{\text{DoF}}=\lceil 2W\rceil+1 describes the aperture-dependent dimension of the ideal band-limited spatial field and is invariant to the number of candidate ports used to discretize the aperture. sections.heading: III Proposed Operator Learning Framework for Continuous SFC Reconstruction
sections.text: In this section, we present the proposed UFNO-based channel estimation framework. We first formulate the channel estimation task as an operator learning problem between infinite-dimensional function spaces to address the continuous aperture nature of FAS. Subsequently, we detail the network architecture design to parameterize this operator efficiently in the spectral domain.

sections.heading: III-A Operator Learning Formulation
sections.text: We propose a resolution-invariant operator framework to map sparse pilot observations to continuous SFC fields, employing the FNO as the underlying architecture. To formalize the problem, let 𝒟 \mathcal{D} denote the bounded continuous spatio-frequency domain. We define the input space 𝒜 = 𝒜 ⁡ ( 𝒟 , ℝ d a ) \mathcal{A}=\mathcal{A}(\mathcal{D};\mathbb{R}^{d_{a}}) consisting of sparse, noisy observation functions, and the output space 𝒰 = 𝒰 ⁡ ( 𝒟 , ℝ d u ) \mathcal{U}=\mathcal{U}(\mathcal{D};\mathbb{R}^{d_{u}}) comprising the corresponding ground-truth continuous channel fields, both are modeled as separable Banach spaces. Our objective is to optimize a continuous-field operator 𝒢 𝚯 : 𝒜 → 𝒰 \mathcal{G}_{\boldsymbol{\Theta}}:\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{U} that approximates the inverse mapping from the observation space to the SPDE solution manifold, where the optimal parameters 𝚯 ∗ \boldsymbol{\Theta}^{*} are determined by minimizing the following expectation arg ⁡ min 𝚯 \displaystyle\arg\min_{\boldsymbol{\Theta}} 𝔼 H ∼ μ , 𝐧 ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , σ 2 ​ 𝐈 ) ​ [ ‖ 𝒢 𝚯 ​ ( 𝒫 ⁡ ( H ) + 𝐧 ) − H ‖ 𝒰 2 ] \displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{H\sim\mu,\,\mathbf{n}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2}\mathbf{I})}\left[\|\mathcal{G}_{\boldsymbol{\Theta}}(\mathcal{P}(H)+\mathbf{n})-H\|_{\mathcal{U}}^{2}\right] (12) + α ​ ℛ ​ ( 𝚯 ) , \displaystyle+\alpha\mathcal{R}(\boldsymbol{\Theta}), where μ \mu denotes the probability measure of the random channel field H ⁡ ( s , f ) H(s,f) , ∥ ⋅ ∥ 𝒰 \|\cdot\|_{\mathcal{U}} denotes the L 2 L^{2} -norm on the functional space, and ℛ ⁡ ( 𝚯 ) \mathcal{R}(\boldsymbol{\Theta}) is a regularization term. As compared to conventional vector-to-vector regression models, the FNO more naturally captures the continuous nature of the SFC. Its spectral convolution provides a non-local parameterization of the reconstruction operator motivated by the Green’s-function representation in ( 11 ). That is, if we modify the spatial sampling grid or increase the port density of the FAS during inference, the neural network should output a consistent continuous channel field H ⁡ ( s , f ) H(s,f) without requiring retraining. Here, resolution invariance means that a learned operator can be evaluated on spatial–frequency discretizations unseen during training, enabling direct cross-resolution channel reconstruction without resolution-specific retraining or explicit output interpolation. The finite-aperture spectral structure further motivates spectral-domain reconstruction, while the learnable threshold introduced below suppresses weak, noise-dominated spectral coefficients. sections.heading: III-B UFNO Architecture Design
sections.text: We now detail the end-to-end architecture of the proposed UFNO framework. It consists of 2 ​ P 2P blocks, where the first P P blocks form a down-sampling path to extract multi-scale features, and the subsequent P P blocks constitute an up-sampling path to reconstruct the high-resolution channel field. The architecture is designed to map the sparse pilot observations to the continuous SFC field through three sequential stages: state initialization, dual-branch representation learning, and multi-scale field projection.

sections.heading: III-B 1 State initialization
sections.text: : The data flow begins with the construction of a high-dimensional input tensor from the sparse and noisy observations 𝐲 obs ∈ ℂ M \mathbf{y}_{\text{obs}}\in\mathbb{C}^{M} . Specifically, let N s N_{s} denote the number of spatial grid points, the input is structured into a multi-channel tensor 𝐗 ∈ ℝ N s × N f × 6 \mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{N_{s}\times N_{f}\times 6} , which encapsulates: 1) the real and imaginary components on the observed pilots; 2) a binary mask identifying the sampled ports; 3) the normalized spatial-frequency grid ( s , f ) (s,f) to encode spatial phase references; and 4) a local SNR indicator. Subsequently, a point-wise lifting layer 𝒫 : ℝ 6 → ℝ d h \mathcal{P}:\mathbb{R}^{6}\to\mathbb{R}^{d_{h}} is applied to project these raw features into a higher-dimensional latent space of dimension d h d_{h} , which can be expressed as v 0 ​ ( s , f ) = GELU ⁡ ( 𝐖 up ​ 𝐗 ​ ( s , f ) + 𝐛 up ) , v_{0}(s,f)=\operatorname{GELU}(\mathbf{W}_{\text{up}}\mathbf{X}(s,f)+\mathbf{b}_{\text{up}}), (13) where 𝐖 up \mathbf{W}_{\text{up}} and 𝐛 up \mathbf{b}_{\text{up}} denote the learnable weight matrix and bias vector, respectively, and GELU ⁡ ( x ) = x ⋅ Φ ⁡ ( x ) \operatorname{GELU}(x)=x\cdot\Phi(x) is the gaussian error linear unit activation [ 30 ] , with Φ ⁡ ( ⋅ ) \Phi(\cdot) denoting the standard gaussian cumulative distribution function. Specifically, GELU ⁡ ( ⋅ ) \operatorname{GELU}(\cdot) provides a smooth transition in the pointwise nonlinear branch rather than the derivative discontinuity of ReLU at the origin, which is generally adopted for derivative-sensitive supervision. To mitigate the aperiodic boundary artifacts inherent in the subsequent fast Fourier transform (FFT) operations, the lifted tensor v 0 v_{0} is dynamically zero-padded along both the spatial and frequency dimensions. This dynamic padding mechanism provides the framework with size adaptability, enabling it to seamlessly process inputs of varying aperture lengths and subcarrier numbers. An ablation over 5,120 5{,}120 test channels shows that removing the padding degrades the overall, boundary-region, and interior NMSE by 1.45 1.45 , 1.59 1.59 , and 1.33 1.33 dB, respectively, confirming that the resulting edge ringing is strongest near the boundaries but also propagates into the interior through the global spectral operator.

sections.heading: III-B 2 Dual-Branch Fourier Representation Learning
sections.text: : Following the initialization, the padded representation tensor v 0 ∈ ℝ S ′ × F ′ × d h v_{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{S^{\prime}\times F^{\prime}\times d_{h}} (where S ′ S^{\prime} and F ′ F^{\prime} denote the dynamically padded spatial and frequency dimensions, respectively) is fed into a cascade of stacked Fourier blocks. These blocks serve as the core representation learning engine of the UFNO. Each block employs a dual-branch structure to concurrently process the global wave propagation and local scattering details. For the l l -th layer, the representation tensor v l ∈ ℝ S ′ × F ′ × d h v_{l}\in\mathbb{R}^{S^{\prime}\times F^{\prime}\times d_{h}} is updated as v l + 1 = InstanceNorm ⁡ ( σ ⁡ ( 𝒦 global ​ ( v l ) + 𝒲 local ​ ( v l ) ) ) , v_{l+1}=\operatorname{InstanceNorm}\left(\sigma(\mathcal{K}_{\text{global}}(v_{l})+\mathcal{W}_{\text{local}}(v_{l}))\right), where σ ⁡ ( ⋅ ) \sigma(\cdot) is a non-linear activation function, and InstanceNorm ⁡ ( ⋅ ) \operatorname{InstanceNorm}(\cdot) denotes the instance normalization operation applied across the spatial-frequency dimensions. The two parallel branches are meticulously parameterized and physically interpreted as follows: ∙ \bullet Global Spectral Branch 𝒦 global ​ ( ⋅ ) \mathcal{K}_{\text{global}}(\cdot) : This branch implements a parameterized integral operator in the wavenumber domain, designed to extract global macroscopic scattering features. To filter high-frequency noise and align with the physical constraints of the propagation environment, the branch first maps the latent representation v l v_{l} into the spectral domain through a spectral convolution pipeline (denoted by 𝒱 l = ℱ mix ​ ( v l ) \mathcal{V}_{l}=\mathcal{F}_{\text{mix}}(v_{l}) ), where we apply a real-to-complex transform on the frequency axis and a Fourier transform on the spatial axis. To reduce computational complexity and suppress out-of-band components, we retain a low-mode subset of the mixed spectrum, i.e., Trunc ​ ( 𝒱 l ) \text{Trunc}(\mathcal{V}_{l}) with spatial and frequency mode budgets. The implementation parameter K s side K_{s}^{\rm side} denotes the number of retained spatial Fourier coefficients on each side of the spectrum, and K s total = 2 ​ K s side K_{s}^{\rm total}=2K_{s}^{\rm side} denotes the corresponding total two-sided budget; K f K_{f} denotes the retained frequency-mode budget. The aperture-dependent N DoF N_{\rm DoF} in Lemma 1 provides a physical reference for selecting K s total K_{s}^{\rm total} . Because the finite-aperture singular functions and the discrete Fourier coefficients are different bases, and because useful recovery also depends on SNR and learned representation capacity, we do not impose K s total = N DoF K_{s}^{\rm total}=N_{\rm DoF} as an exact design rule. The retained modes then undergo a learnable complex linear mixing followed by a sparse-promoting denoising operation. To further enhance robustness against in-band receiver noise, we introduce a learnable spectral soft-thresholding (SST) mechanism, 𝒮 𝜸 ​ ( ⋅ ) \mathcal{S}_{\boldsymbol{\gamma}}(\cdot) . Here, mode truncation provides explicit low-pass support, while SST performs amplitude-adaptive shrinkage to suppress low-energy coefficients that are typically noise-dominated. The global spectral operation is formulated as: 𝒦 global ​ ( v l ) = ℱ mix − 1 ​ ( 𝒮 𝜸 ​ ( 𝐖 ⊛ Trunc ​ ( 𝒱 l ) ) ) , \mathcal{K}_{\text{global}}(v_{l})=\mathcal{F}^{-1}_{\text{mix}}\left(\mathcal{S}_{\boldsymbol{\gamma}}\left(\mathbf{W}\circledast\text{Trunc}(\mathcal{V}_{l})\right)\right), (14) where ⊛ \circledast denotes complex-valued tensor contraction (e.g., Einstein summation) across latent dimensions, and ℱ mix − 1 ​ ( ⋅ ) \mathcal{F}^{-1}_{\text{mix}}(\cdot) denotes the inverse mixed transform back to the spatial-frequency grid. The element-wise SST operator 𝒮 𝜸 ​ ( ⋅ ) \mathcal{S}_{\boldsymbol{\gamma}}(\cdot) for a complex spectral entry 𝐙 \mathbf{Z} is: 𝒮 𝜸 ​ ( 𝐙 ) = 𝐙 ⋅ max ⁡ ( 0 , 1 − 𝜸 | Z | + ϵ ) , \mathcal{S}_{\boldsymbol{\gamma}}(\mathbf{Z})=\mathbf{Z}\cdot\max\left(0,1-\frac{\boldsymbol{\gamma}}{|Z|+\epsilon}\right), (15) where 𝜸 ∈ ℝ + \boldsymbol{\gamma}\in\mathbb{R}_{+} is a learnable scalar threshold shared across channels and modes, and ϵ \epsilon is a small constant for numerical stability. By integrating this sparsity-inducing threshold into the wavenumber domain, UFNO adaptively suppresses weak, noise-dominated spectral coefficients while retaining the dominant global scattering structure. ∙ \bullet Local MLP Branch 𝒲 local ​ ( ⋅ ) \mathcal{W}_{\text{local}}(\cdot) : In parallel, a point-wise multi-layer perceptron (MLP), implemented via 1 × 1 1\times 1 convolutions, operates strictly along the channel dimension ℝ d h → ℝ d h \mathbb{R}^{d_{h}}\to\mathbb{R}^{d_{h}} without expanding the receptive field. While the spectral branch models non-local spatial–frequency dependencies, spectral truncation can attenuate fine-scale variations. The local branch complements it by representing residual local channel structure and nonlinear feature transformations that are not captured by the retained spectral coefficients. Compared with standard CNNs or fully connected networks, the UFNO more naturally captures the fundamental physics of electromagnetic wave propagation. By explicitly embedding the integral operator structure into the neural architecture, the UFNO is better equipped to model the non-local interactions characteristic of scattering environments. In particular, while a standard convolutional layer is limited by a small local receptive field (e.g., 3 × 3 3\times 3 kernels), the Fourier layer in the UFNO performs multiplication in the spectral domain, which is mathematically equivalent to a global convolution in the spatial domain. This mechanism enables every point in the reconstructed field to instantaneously aggregate information from the entire aperture, effectively mimicking the Huygens-Fresnel principle, where the field at any point is a superposition of wavelets from all sources. Remark 3 . In practical wireless scenarios, sparse observations and additive white Gaussian noise (AWGN) inevitably introduce spurious high-frequency aliasing. The proposed SST operation adaptively filters out low-amplitude spectral components, effectively denoising the SFC field by constraining the solution to reside on the physical wave manifold.

sections.heading: III-B 3 U-Shaped Multiscale Fusion
sections.text: To construct the complete continuous field, the aforementioned Fourier blocks are organized into a symmetric encoder-decoder U-shaped architecture. During the encoding phase, successive SST operations act as sequential low-pass filters, extracting the coarse-grained, low-frequency eigen-modes (e.g., macroscopic angles of arrival and large-scale shadowing). During the decoding phase, symmetric skip connections are employed to prevent the attenuation of high-frequency local variations. Specifically, the feature map from the l l -th encoder layer is directly added to the input of the corresponding decoder layer: v dec ( l ) = ℋ block ​ ( v dec ( l − 1 ) + v enc ( P − l ) ) , v_{\text{dec}}^{(l)}=\mathcal{H}_{\text{block}}\left(v_{\text{dec}}^{(l-1)}+v_{\text{enc}}^{(P-l)}\right), (16) where ℋ block ​ ( ⋅ ) \mathcal{H}_{\text{block}}(\cdot) denotes the FNO block in the decoder, and P P is the total number of encoder layers. This multi-scale fusion strategy ensures that the precise spatial phase alignment and sub-wavelength small-scale fading details are organically fused with the global scattering structures. In the final stage, the reconstructed tensor is cropped back to its original physical dimensions to remove the padded boundaries. An MLP-based projection head 𝒬 : ℝ d h → ℝ 2 \mathcal{Q}:\mathbb{R}^{d_{h}}\to\mathbb{R}^{2} is then applied point-wise to map the high-dimensional latent vectors back to the physical SFC domain.

sections.heading: IV-C Performance Comparison
sections.text: Fig. 3: NMSE comparison under varying SNR. Fig. 4: NMSE comparison under varying delay spreads (OOD robustness test). The performance of the proposed UFNO and the benchmark methods is evaluated in terms of the normalized mean squared error (NMSE) between the reconstructed channel H ^ \hat{H} and the ground truth H H , defined as NMSE ​ ( H ^ , H ) = 10 ​ log 10 ⁡ ( ‖ H − H ^ ‖ F 2 ‖ H ‖ F 2 ) . \text{NMSE}(\hat{H},H)=10\log_{10}\left(\frac{\|H-\hat{H}\|_{F}^{2}}{\|H\|_{F}^{2}}\right). (21) Fig. 3 illustrates the NMSE performance across a wide range of SNR levels, where the proposed UFNO consistently maintains a superior performance envelope. While learning-based architectures significantly surpass traditional model-driven methods by effectively leveraging data-driven field priors, UFNO demonstrates the most robust scaling behavior as the SNR increases. Although UFNO and ViT achieve comparable NMSE in the extremely low-SNR regime, UFNO exhibits a significantly more pronounced performance gain as the noise floor drops, achieving an NMSE below − 35 -35 dB at 30 30 dB SNR and outperforming the ViT and CNN baselines by over 5 5 dB. The efficacy of our architectural innovations is further elucidated by the performance of the ablated variants in high-SNR environments. As shown in Fig. 3 , the full UFNO begins to diverge from UFNO w/o SST for SNR > 10 >10 dB, reaching a 3 3 dB performance margin at 30 30 dB. Similarly, UFNO w/o S-Loss trails the full architecture by approximately 3 3 dB in the high-SNR regime. These results suggest that while SST is instrumental in adaptively suppressing high-frequency spectral leakage that would otherwise be masked by noise, the Sobolev loss is critical for preserving high-gradient field structures and averting accuracy saturation as the observation quality improves. Fig. 4 further evaluates the robustness under increasing delay spread. Physically, a larger delay spread induces faster phase rotations across the frequency domain, intrinsically intensifying the frequency selectivity. Under a fixed sampling ratio, this stronger frequency selectivity increases the number of significant frequency-domain components and worsens the conditioning of the underdetermined inverse problem; it does not change the spatial EDoF in ( 9 ), which is determined by the aperture. Crucially, as the learning-based models are trained solely on a nominal 300 300 ns delay spread, shifting to extremes (e.g., 800 800 ns) introduces an out-of-distribution (OOD) shift. Interestingly, CNN exhibits extreme robustness (a nearly flat curve), acting as a localized nonlinear interpolator: its local receptive fields are insensitive to global phase variations, preventing severe OOD collapse albeit at the cost of a poor baseline performance. In contrast, models capturing global dependencies ( ViT and UFNO) experience more noticeable degradation under the extreme 800 800 ns regime. For UFNO, this behavior is physically interpretable: at enormous delay spreads, the rapid frequency responses shift the intrinsic signal energy into higher spectral modes. Consequently, the low-pass mode truncation mechanism (e.g., K f = 16 K_{f}=16 ) inherently cuts off these emerging high-frequency channel components. We observe that removing either the SST or Sobolev loss modules compromises reconstruction stability as the delay spread deviates from the training set. Notably, UFNO w/o S-Loss exhibits the most pronounced degradation in the high-delay regime (e.g., around 800 800 ns), indicating that physics-aware gradient regularization is vital for maintaining field consistency beyond nominal conditions. Nevertheless, the full UFNO maintains a dominant performance advantage over ViT and CNN architectures across the 100 100 ns to 500 500 ns range. Compared to classical CS-based methods, our framework provides consistent, multi-order-of-magnitude NMSE improvements over the entire evaluated domain, demonstrating the superior generalization power of physics-informed operator learning in complex EM environments.

Each point on this curve reports the complex NMSE averaged over 5,120 5{,}120 independently generated test channels. In extremely sparse regimes, the limited resource-block is fundamentally insufficient to capture the underlying channel manifold, leading to severe ambiguity for all estimators. As the sampling ratio increases, traditional model-driven methods struggle to show continuous proportional improvements. Specifically, the LS baseline exhibits a nearly flat trajectory due to its naive mapping that fails to spatially interpolate the unobservable zero-padded pcoints. Furthermore, compressed sensing methods ( OMP and SBL ) reveal sub-optimal and marginally jagged performance gains; this is primarily attributed to their rigid sparsity hyperparameter constraints (e.g., fixed maximum number of scatter paths) along with the inherent grid-mismatch uncertainty introduced by discrete uniform masking. In contrast, deep learning-based methods exhibit significant performance gains as the sampling ratio increases, particularly as sampling ratio approaches the training distribution limit of 21.7 % 21.7\% . Specifically, at 20 % 20\% , the full model outperforms UFNO w/o SST and UFNO w/o S-Loss by approximately 13 13 – 14 14 dB. This substantial margin underscores the necessity of adaptive spectral truncation and Sobolev-gradient supervision in highly under-determined reconstruction, confirming that the synergistic interplay between spectral manifold partitioning and gradient-level fidelity is critical for capturing fine-grained sub-wavelength structures. Fig. 6 provides qualitative evidence of how reconstruction fidelity evolves with sampling density. As sampling ratio increases from 1 % 1\% to 20 % 20\% , the recovered field transitions from coarse low-frequency envelopes to structured multipath textures with progressively improved stripe orientation and amplitude contrast, with NMSE improving from approximately − 1.9 -1.9 dB to − 29.5 -29.5 dB, indicating that dominant spatio-frequency components become reliably recoverable beyond very sparse sampling.

For each of 512 independently generated channels, the same underlying continuous SFC is evaluated at all spatial–frequency resolutions. All learned estimators are trained only at 48 × 48 48\times 48 and applied without parameter updates or resolution-specific fine-tuning. The controls comprise direct inference by CNN, ViT, and Standard FNO; nearest, linear, and cubic interpolation from the target-resolution sparse pilots; and bilinear or bicubic upsampling of the dense 48 × 48 48\times 48 CNN reconstruction. For the sparse-pilot interpolation baselines, nearest interpolation assigns each unobserved location the value of its closest pilot, whereas linear and cubic interpolation construct piecewise linear and smooth piecewise cubic surfaces, respectively, directly from the observed pilot coordinates. For the upsampling baselines, the CNN first produces a dense 48 × 48 48\times 48 channel estimate; its real and imaginary components are then resized to the target resolution using bilinear interpolation over adjacent output samples or bicubic interpolation over a larger local neighborhood. The former group therefore reconstructs directly from the target-resolution pilots, whereas the latter tests post-processing of a low-resolution learned channel estimate. Across the five unseen resolutions, UFNO achieves an average NMSE of − 29.39 -29.39 dB, with only a 1.28 1.28 dB average loss relative to its native-resolution result. It outperforms direct CNN, linear interpolation, cubic interpolation, and direct Standard FNO by 5.01 5.01 , 7.86 7.86 , 8.32 8.32 , and 21.67 21.67 dB on average, respectively, and exceeds CNN bilinear and bicubic upsampling by 4.90 4.90 and 4.93 4.93 dB. Although both models employ Fourier weights that are independent of the spatial–frequency sampling size, this property permits evaluation on a new discretization but does not guarantee unchanged finite-resolution accuracy. Standard FNO propagates changes in the discrete spectrum of the sparse-pilot input through ten sequential Fourier blocks, whereas UFNO’s symmetric inter-layer skip connections provide short paths for intermediate representations and its SST suppresses low-energy spectral coefficients that are more sensitive to sampling changes and noise. These mechanisms limit the accumulation of discretization mismatch and provide a structural explanation for UFNO’s more stable cross-resolution performance. These controlled comparisons demonstrate the intended benefit of the proposed operator-learning framework: a single frozen UFNO preserves high-fidelity SFC reconstruction across unseen discretizations through direct inference, rather than through resolution-specific retraining or post-hoc resizing. sections.heading: V Conclusion
sections.text: This paper establishes a paradigm shift for broadband FAS channel estimation by reformulating the ill-posed discrete recovery task as a continuous physical field reconstruction problem. The formulation is motivated by the Green’s-function integral structure of the projected Helmholtz model and reveals that spectral reconstruction is fundamentally an inverse deconvolution problem. To address this, we propose the UFNO framework, which incorporates a learnable SST mechanism and a dual-branch architecture to circumvent inherent low-pass spectral biases. Furthermore, a physics-aware Sobolev loss promotes consistency in both channel values and physically meaningful spatial–frequency variations. Extensive numerical results demonstrate that the proposed operator learning framework substantially outperforms both traditional iterative solvers and state-of-the-art deep learning baselines, delivering superior reconstruction fidelity alongside orders-of-magnitude lower inference latency than iterative solvers at high spatial–frequency resolutions . Future work will validate UFNO using measured channels and investigate its integration into practical receivers. Its cross-resolution inference capability may further facilitate deployment with different spatial and frequency sampling resolutions. The framework may also be extended to planar or volumetric FAS configurations. Supporting time-varying channels requires a spatio-temporal operator that captures Doppler effects and temporal correlation. The fixed Fourier-basis representation adopted in the present spatial–frequency formulation may be insufficient to characterize the coupled non-stationarity across these dimensions, and more general tools from harmonic analysis may be useful for developing suitable representations and operators.

Abstract Fluid antenna systems (FAS) leverage continuous reconfigurable apertures to transcend the spatial limits of fixed-position arrays, yet acquiring full-aperture channel state information (CSI) from sparse observations remains a formidable bottleneck. In this paper, we establish a continuous-field formulation for FAS by recasting channel estimation as a stochastic inverse field-reconstruction problem constrained by the projected Helmholtz model. Through electromagnetic information theory (EIT)-based spectral leakage analysis, we demonstrate that finite-aperture reconstruction induces an intrinsic convolutional relationship in the spectral domain, rendering the estimation task a fundamental frequency-domain inverse deconvolution problem. To solve this, we propose a U-shaped Fourier neural operator (UFNO) specifically tailored for noisy, underdetermined wireless environments. Furthermore, we leverage the Landau–Pollak theorem to derive an aperture-dependent EDoF bound that guides the spatial mode budget, and employ a physics-aware Sobolev loss to promote consistency in both channel values and spatial variations. Unlike conventional learning-based approaches, a single frozen UFNO can be directly evaluated at unseen spatial–frequency resolutions without resolution-specific retraining or explicit output interpolation. Extensive simulations show that our framework significantly outperforms state-of-the-art benchmarks in accuracy while achieving orders-of-magnitude lower inference latency than iterative solvers at high spatial–frequency resolutions . Index Terms: Fluid Antenna Systems, channel estimation, Fourier neural operator, physics-informed deep learning, electromagnetic information theory. I Introduction Multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) technology is fundamental to contemporary wireless networks, leveraging spatial degrees of freedom (DoFs) to enhance spectral efficiency and link reliability [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 ] . However, conventional MIMO architectures are inherently limited by the Nyquist-based half-wavelength spacing rule, which restricts spatial diversity gains within a fixed physical aperture regardless of antenna density. To surpass these constraints, continuous-aperture MIMO (CAP-MIMO) has emerged as a transformative paradigm [ 5 , 3 ] . By integrating metasurfaces or dense sub-wavelength arrays, CAP-MIMO enables ultra-fine electromagnetic (EM) control, effectively realizing a holographic radiating aperture [ 5 ] . Nevertheless, translating the theoretical potential of CAP-MIMO into practice is hindered by several interrelated challenges. The extreme proximity of sub-wavelength elements induces severe mutual coupling and complex near-field interactions that complicate signal processing. Furthermore, acquiring full-space EM channel state information (CSI) necessitates high-dimensional channel matrices, where the resulting “curse of dimensionality” imposes prohibitive pilot and computational overheads. These difficulties are compounded by the excessive hardware costs and power consumption associated with scaling active elements, presenting substantial barriers to the large-scale commercialization of dense-array-centric architectures. Against this backdrop, fluid antenna systems (FAS) introduce a transformative paradigm that sidesteps the limitations of static hardware densification [ 6 , 7 , 8 , 9 ] . By enabling a limited number of movable antennas to dynamically traverse a continuous spatial manifold within a predefined aperture, FAS not only minimizes hardware overhead but also circumvents the analytical complexities and hardware redundancy inherent in metasurface-based CAP-MIMO. The seminal work in [ 10 ] first introduced the FAS concept, and demonstrated that even a small linear aperture (e.g., 0.5 λ \lambda ) with sub-wavelength port spacing can yield significant spatial diversity gains, even surpassing multi-antenna MRC systems. Furthermore, the authors in [ 11 ] revealed that FAS can achieve substantial ergodic capacity in both point-to-point and multi-user multiple-access scenarios. However, FAS performance hinges on high-resolution CSI across the full spatial domain, demanding dense sub-wavelength measurements. Hardware constraints permit only a sparse subset, rendering channel estimation a severely underdetermined inverse problem. Considering its sparse nature, a conventional approach is adopting compressed sensing (CS) technology [ 12 , 13 , 14 ] . By sending pilots from the random antenna ports, the channel estimation problem can be formulated as a sparse signal recovery problem, which can be solved by algorithms such as orthogonal matching pursuit (OMP) or sparse Bayesian learning (SBL). For instance, the authors in [ 12 ] proposed a successive transmitter-receiver compressed sensing (STRCS) method by exploiting the angular-domain sparsity of multi-path components to reconstruct the continuous field-response information from finite measurements. The authors in [ 13 ] developed an SBL-based channel estimator by reformulating the estimation task into a basis selection problem, thereby achieving superior reconstruction accuracy with limited radio-frequency chains. However, these methods are fundamentally limited by the discretization of the channel into a finite grid, leading to grid mismatch artifacts and high computational complexity in high-dimensional scenarios. Besides, these methods highly rely on the sparsity assumption based on the shallow scattering environment, leading to limited implementation cases. Conversely, learning-based approaches leverage data-driven architectures to characterize the nonlinear mapping from sparse pilot observations to full-space channel realizations, thereby shifting the burden of computationally intensive iterations to low-latency feed-forward inference. Beyond conventional neural network-driven channel extrapolation, which seeks to learn direct mappings from sparse inputs to high-dimensional CSI, the reconstruction of the channel field via generative modeling has emerged as a pivotal research frontier. Frameworks such as diffusion models [ 15 ] , conditional generative adversarial networks (cGANs) [ 16 ] , and variational autoencoders (VAEs) [ 17 ] reformulate channel estimation as an inverse problem regularized by learned implicit priors. These methods have demonstrated a superior capacity for capturing intricate electromagnetic (EM) characteristics and spatial correlations at sub-wavelength scales. Despite their reconstructive fidelity, diffusion-based methods necessitate multi-step iterative sampling, which incurs substantial computational latency. This delay poses a significant challenge in satisfying the stringent constraints of the channel coherence interval, particularly in high-mobility scenarios. Furthermore, while techniques based on 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS), such as RF-PGS [ 18 ] , RF-3DGS [ 19 ] , facilitate rapid rendering and geometric alignment, they are fundamentally limited to site-specific optimization. These approaches lack the generalization capability required for inference in unseen environments and often neglect the underlying physical operator constraints governing electromagnetic wave propagation. Grounded in electromagnetic information theory (EIT) [ 5 , 20 , 21 , 22 ] , wireless channels are fundamentally modeled as continuous physical fields governed by Maxwell’s equations and the associated Helmholtz equation, rather than as collections of isolated random variables. Although these fields exhibit an inherent low-rank structure in the wavenumber domain, existing solution methodologies encounter significant technical barriers. Specifically, numerical solvers, e.g., ray tracing, the finite element method, and the finite-difference method, are often computationally prohibitive. Moreover, they are constrained by a prohibitive trade-off between computational accuracy and efficiency, making them ill-suited for the millisecond-level real-time reconstruction required by 6G networks. Alternatively, statistical kernel-based approaches [ 20 ] , including Gaussian process regression and kernel learning, have introduced physically inspired kernels, such as the electromagnetic correlation function. However, these methods essentially rely on fixed-kernel structures, which lead to high computational complexity for matrix inversion and struggle to adapt to complex, dynamic EM environments. Furthermore, most existing techniques lack resolution invariance, limiting direct channel reconstruction at spatial–frequency discretizations unseen during training. Inspired by the paradigm shift toward neural operator learning for partial differential equations (PDEs) [ 23 ] , we propose a physics-informed learning framework tailored for FAS channel estimation. Unlike deterministic and noise-free PDE benchmarks where Fourier Neural Operators (FNOs) excel, FAS estimation presents an ill-posed inverse problem with an unknown stochastic excitation and severely undersampled observations. Standard FNOs can not be directly implemented for this problem due to their rigid spectral truncation, which lacks adaptability to varying noise levels, and a pervasive low-pass bias that suppresses critical sub-wavelength spatial features. To address these challenges, we reformulate FAS channel estimation as a continuous operator learning task and introduce a U-shaped FNO (UFNO) whose non-local architecture is motivated by the projected Helmholtz model. The primary contributions of this work are summarized as follows. ∙ \bullet We recast FAS channel estimation as a stochastic inverse field-reconstruction problem constrained by the projected Helmholtz model. By shifting from discrete vector recovery to continuous field reconstruction, we utilize EIT to reveal that finite-aperture sensing induces an intrinsic spectral convolution. This analysis formalizes the channel estimation task as an inverse deconvolution problem within the spatio-frequency domain. ∙ \bullet Beyond empirical modeling, we derive a closed-form upper bound on the effective degrees of freedom (EDoF) of the FAS channel via the Landau–Pollak theorem. This result characterizes the aperture-dependent spatial dimensionality and provides a physics-based reference for selecting the UFNO spatial mode budget. We further distinguish this ideal dimension count from SNR-dependent stable recovery through a finite-aperture singular-value analysis and multi-aperture simulations. ∙ \bullet We develop a UFNO based channel estimation framework to overcome the limitations of conventional operators through two key mechanisms. First, a learnable soft-thresholding operator is introduced to dynamically suppress noise while preserving physical signal modes across varying signal-to-noise ratios (SNRs). Second, a dual-branch spectral-spatial structure is employed to mitigate low-pass bias, enabling the simultaneous capture of macroscopic low-frequency structures and high-frequency sub-wavelength details. ∙ \bullet We propose a physics-aware Sobolev loss that penalizes discrepancies in both channel values and spatial–frequency variations. This regularization enhances the recovery of high-gradient scattering structures. Numerical results demonstrate that our framework achieves grid-agnostic reconstruction with orders-of-magnitude lower latency than model-based baselines. Finally, Section V concludes the paper.
